23.0.s.en: 1. Etiquette of sitting at a ruler’s table

23.0.0.en: 1 When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee: 2 And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite. 3 Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are bread of lies.

23.0.1.en: When thou sittest to eat with a ruler, consider diligently what is before thee [1].

23.0.2.en: Many rejoice that they find favor with the ruler, enter with him into an almost familial relationship, and share with him at his table. But it is fitting for a person, however firmly his relationship with the ruler is established, to recognize his limits; if he sits with him at the table, let him consider that he is in the presence of a ruler, and not take advantage of his love, but give honour to whom honour is due (Rom 13:7).

23.0.3.en: St. Evagrius sees that if a person must be careful when he sits with a ruler, then all the more must he be careful when he reads the Holy Bible as the royal table, contemplating it in a spiritual, intellectual way, for understanding it in a literal way does not give us the truth. Many of the Fathers see that this table is the table of the Eucharist.

23.0.4.en: * “When thou sittest to eat with the ruler, understand with discernment what is before thee.” Christ has already been proclaimed as the Ruler; His table and food are the words of His teaching about the eternal good things. He who understands with discernment what Jesus teaches by His works and words stretches out his hand, which means his works, and begins to show that he imitates Christ, becoming humble, peaceable, loving to all, patient in trials. He who does not do this, but instead looks eagerly toward the pleasures of the world, must cease to desire temporal goods, which are the mark of the vain life, and whoever loves them will not enjoy the eternal possessions.

23.0.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * What is the “table of the one in authority (the ruler)” but the mind of him who said: “I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me” (Phil 4:13), “when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Cor 12:10)? On the table of this pure man of authority, that is, in his heart and in his mind, bread is offered to the Lord.

23.0.6.en: If you sit at the table of this Apostle who has authority, it is that you may understand with discernment what is set before you, that is, understand spiritually what he says.

23.0.7.en: Origen * The Holy Scriptures alert us to partake with discernment of the table when we are invited to eat at the table of a rich man. I can say that the table of the Holy Bible, which belongs to the Rich One, is set before us. We enter a garden filled with roses; here a rose, there a lily gleaming with whiteness; in every place there are many kinds of flowers.

23.0.8.en: St. Jerome * What is “the ruler’s table” but the table from which we partake of the Body and Blood of Him who gave His life for us? And what is sitting but approaching in humility? And what is considering and understanding the things set before you but being made worthy to receive so great a grace as this?

23.0.9.en: * You are approaching the table of the ruler. You who are believers know to what table you are approaching. To what royal table you are approaching.

23.0.10.en: What is set before you is not a table made by the skill of cooks. Christ Himself sets His table, and He satisfies you. Be poor, and you will receive your fill.

23.0.11.en: * Certainly it is a great table, where the Lord of the table Himself is the feast. No one feeds his guests with himself as food. But Christ the Lord did this, being Himself the Host, and Himself the food and drink.

23.1.0.en: St. Augustine And put a knife to thy throat, if thou be a man given to appetite [2].

23.1.1.en: It is fitting for a person not to be gluttonous, but to eat in order to live, and not to live in order to eat and take pleasure in food. How much more when he sits at the table of a ruler, for his sitting with the ruler is loftier and more delightful than the desire for food.

23.1.2.en: If this is so with regard to sitting with a ruler, how much more when you are in the presence of the King of kings and Lord of lords, for there is no pleasure of food or drink, or preoccupation with luxurious clothing, or luxury, or frivolous laughter that should draw us away from the sweetness of sitting with Him.

23.1.3.en: * Hear then, my beloved, to whom I write, I mean what concerns the hermits, monks, virgins and saints. Above all it is fitting for the man upon whom the yoke has been placed to be firm in his faith. And as I wrote to you in the first epistle, he must be zealous in fasting and prayer, fervent in the love of Christ, humble, meek and wise. Let his speech be calm and cheerful, and his mind sincere toward all. Let him weigh the words he utters, and make a fence for his mouth that turns it away from harmful words, and let him keep entirely away from frivolous laughter.

23.1.4.en: May he not love showy clothing, and it is not fitting for him to grow his hair long and adorn it and anoint it with perfumes.

23.1.5.en: May he not run after banquets, nor wear luxurious clothes.

23.1.6.en: Let him not presume to drink more wine.

23.2.0.en: St. Aphrahat Be not desirous of his dainties: for they are bread of lies [3].

23.2.1.en: Daniel and his three young companions give us living examples of not desiring the king’s dainties. For since they did not indulge themselves in the dainties, “God gave them knowledge and skill in all learning and wisdom: and Daniel had understanding in all visions and dreams” (Dan 1:17).

23.2.2.en: * There is no limit to the gluttony practiced by these people. Truly, in the constant invention of a multitude of new sweets and the search for recipes for foods, they are ruined amid pastries and honey cakes and sweets...

23.2.3.en: A man of this kind (a glutton) is nothing but a huge mouth... But as for us, who seek the heavenly food, we must control our bellies and keep them under the watch of heaven.

23.2.4.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * Beware of gluttony! Do not be bound to your appetite, for it drives the fear of God out of the heart and modesty out of the face, makes a man captive to perishable, base passions, and leads the mind astray from God. Let your eating be for the sustenance of the body and not for appetite, make it weak (feeble) a little, and tire it much with prostrations (metanoia).

23.2.5.en: Abba Anthony the Great * Do not go to the feasts of the saints and eat and drink and make merry, for it was gluttony that drove Adam out of Paradise.

23.2.6.en: St. Abba Isaiah * The beginning of all goodness is spiritual love, followed by humility and the love of poverty and the cutting off of familiarity. But the ruin of the soul is the love of the belly.

23.2.7.en: St. Abba Pishoy * Eating with appetite is desiring to take food not for the need of the body but because of gluttony. But if a man sees that for a right motive (such as the health of the body) he prefers, for example, green vegetables to dry legumes, this is not for the sake of appetite but because they are lighter (that is, easier to digest); then the case is different.

23.3.s.en: 2. Freeing the heart from the desire for wealth

23.3.0.en: 4 Labour not to be rich: cease from thine own wisdom. 5 Wilt thou make thine eyes fly toward it, and it is not? for it maketh itself wings; as an eagle it flieth toward heaven.

23.3.3.en: Some reckon it to be prudence or wisdom for people to spend all their effort or energies to become rich, so they gather money greedily and not from inner satisfaction. These make wealth a god to whom they bow in worship, just as gluttons make their bellies gods. Both labor without rest, and the world uses them instead of their using it.

23.3.4.en: Wilt thou make thine eyes fly toward it, and it is not?

23.4.0.en: As an eagle it flieth toward heaven [5].

23.4.1.en: The wise man likens the greedy to those who set up wings for wealth, not that it may fly with them to rest, but that it may fly away from them and vanish, so that they do not find what they had gathered. Whereas the contented man who uses the world well carries the two wings of the Spirit to fly as it were to heaven, while the labor of the greedy man’s hands flies away from him, and he is left cast down in the world in dire want!

23.4.2.en: When Gehazi, the disciple of the prophet Elisha, was enslaved by the love of money, he ran after Naaman the Syrian to take something from him (2 Kgs 5:2), and he received double what he asked, but Naaman’s leprosy clung to him and to his seed also (2 Kgs 5:27). And when Achan the son of Carmi coveted a goodly Babylonish garment and two hundred shekels of silver and a wedge of gold (Josh 7:21), the wrath of God came upon the whole people because of him.

23.4.3.en: * You cannot live according to God if you love money and earthly pleasures.

23.4.4.en: St. Abba Isidore * Listen to me, my brother, and bear with an opinion from me that may profit you: you are tempted by the demon of covetousness and the love of money, for I have seen it in you; but if you accept my advice and drive it out of your heart, you will complete the work of God perfectly in this place, and in the end you will be glorified, and God’s chastisements will not come near you. But if you do not listen to me, you will fall into what Gehazi fell into, because his disease is in you!

23.4.5.en: * I tell you, my son, that every evil work is in these two things: fornication and the love of money, although fornication is very evil, and after a little while a man turns his face away from it and is disgusted by it because of its foul smell. But the love of money comes from hoarding, and when it comes it is sweet to you, because it is greedy and insatiable; for this reason a man must seal the doors of the church of the wilderness and the doors of the dead with fear of the powers of this age, for in truth certain men will arise who search and inquire into the inheritance of those who sleep, forgetting what is written: “If riches increase, set not your heart upon them” (Ps 62:10) LXX, and this is what the Apostle speaks of: “The love of money is the root of all evil” (1 Tim 6:10).

23.5.0.en: 6 Eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye, neither desire thou his dainty meats: 7 For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he: Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee. 8 The morsel which thou hast eaten shalt thou vomit up, and lose thy sweet words. 9 Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words.

23.5.1.en: Eat thou not the bread of him that hath an evil eye, neither desire thou his dainty meats [6].

23.5.2.en: While we love all humanity from all the heart, this love must be in the Lord, practiced in a spirit of wisdom, so that it is for our edification and the edification of others. But whoever befriends the wicked to share their pleasures and lusts, drives his life toward destruction.

23.5.3.en: * Wise is he who forbids us to eat in the company of an envious man, and in his reference to this company at the table, this applies also to every other social relationship. Just as we must be careful in material matters that can easily catch fire, and keep as far from the fire as possible, so it is fitting for us to refrain as far as we can from forming friendships in all circles in which the envious are members. By doing this we keep ourselves out of range of their spears. For we are caught in the troubles of envy only when we draw near to it.

23.5.4.en: St. Cyril the Great For as he thinketh in his heart, so is he.

23.6.0.en: Eat and drink, saith he to thee; but his heart is not with thee [7].

23.7.0.en: The wise man calls us to flee from the table of the wicked man, for while he offers you food and drink he carries no true love within him; rather, what concerns him is the cost of the table he has set before you, or how he can exploit the offering of the feast to push you toward evil, The morsel which thou hast eaten shalt thou vomit up, and lose thy sweet words [8].

23.7.1.en: When a person discovers that the wicked friend offers his table but not his heart, and that his honeyed words hide bad feelings, he cannot stand the food offered to him but vomits it up.

23.7.2.en: * Do not corrupt the commandment of God for the sake of anyone’s friendship.

23.7.3.en: St. Anthony the Great * If you have a friendship with one of the brethren, and your mind reproaches you that your association with him harms you, cut yourself off from him. And I say this, beloved, not so that you may hate people, but so that you may cut off the causes of vice.

23.7.4.en: St. Ephrem the Syrian * Let us follow the friendships that are according to the Spirit, for they are strong and hard to dissolve, and not the friendships that are formed around the table.

23.7.5.en: St. John Chrysostom * Do not bind yourself in friendship with any person except your poor brethren; do not hasten to any person for him to do you good, but hasten to God alone and care for His service, for it is He who gathers you into the bowels of His fatherhood. But as for you, beware of familiarity with people, and let all your familiarity be only between you and God. Do not hasten to any person to enjoy rest in your familiarity with him; do not presume upon his dwelling, and do not stay with him without receiving an order to do so, lest you be a burden to him. My brother, if you wish to be at rest all your life, and to have your thoughts united with God every hour, beware of familiarity with people.

23.8.0.en: St. Macarius the Great Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words [9].

23.8.1.en: The foolish man who persists in his folly in stubbornness stops his ears from listening to any counsel, so it is fitting for the wise man not to waste his time giving him advice. As the Lord Christ says: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you” (Mt 7:6).

23.8.2.en: * We can understand “that which is holy” and “pearls” as one thing, called holy because of the obligation not to corrupt it, and pearls because of the obligation not to despise it. For a man corrupts what he does not wish to keep whole, and despises what he reckons trifling and base. Therefore a despised thing is said to be trampled under feet. The Lord says: “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs,” because dogs rush upon a thing to tear it, even if this thing cannot be torn, corrupted or defiled. Let us then consider what these violent and fiercely hostile opponents of the Spirit desire. They desire to destroy the truth, which cannot be destroyed. But swine differ from dogs, for they do not attack to tear with their teeth, but they defile the thing by trampling it with their feet in recklessness... Let us then understand that the “dogs” signify the opponents of the truth, and the “swine” those who despise it.

23.8.3.en: St. Augustine * Take care lest you be led into teaching while you are young, and go astray through vainglory, and do not teach what you have learned by experience, more than by reading, to those who have been defiled to the end (that is, the reckless), so that what the wise man Solomon declared is fulfilled, who said: “Speak not in the ears of a fool: for he will despise the wisdom of thy words” (Prov 9:23). And “Give not that which is holy unto the dogs, neither cast ye your pearls before swine, lest they trample them under their feet, and turn again and rend you” (Mt 6:7). It is fitting for us to hide the secrets of the spiritual meanings from people of this kind, so that we may truly sing: “Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee” (Ps 11:119).

23.9.0.en: Remove not the old landmark; and enter not into the fields of the fatherless [10].

23.10.0.en: He shall plead their cause with thee [11].

23.10.1.en: Whoever wrongs widows, orphans, the weak and those unable to defend themselves defies God Himself, their Creator and living Redeemer. He pleads their cause, defends them, and restores their rights to them.

23.10.2.en: Queen Jezebel killed poor Naboth the Jezreelite and inherited his vineyard (1 Kgs 21), and she thought that there was no one who could defend him, but the dogs ate her in the very field of Jezreel that she had seized (2 Kgs 9).

23.11.0.en: 12 Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge. 13 Withhold not correction from the child: for if thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die. 14 Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell.

23.11.1.en: Apply thine heart unto instruction, and thine ears to the words of knowledge [12].

23.11.2.en: Kail and Deiltesch see that this proverb is a summary or echo of what is stated in (Prov 22:17-21), and as for the word “instruction” here, in their opinion it refers to discipline, whether from God or from human beings in moderation.

23.11.3.en: This advice is general, directed to the old as to the young, to those who need to learn and to those who are already learned. We all need God’s plan and His dealings with us even when they seem firm, just as we need guiding fathers, so that we may incline our ears to the words of knowledge in a spirit of humility.

23.11.4.en: In the discourse of St. Gregory, head of the hermits of Cyprus, he likens this holy knowledge to the yoke (the part of the plow that is placed on the neck of the ox); without it the soil of the heart will not be plowed to bear the fruits of the Spirit.

23.11.5.en: * The yoke with which these holy farmers toil is the holy knowledge, composed of three divine virtues, namely love, fasting and prayer, or faith, hope and love, and the furrow in which this plow goes to cleave the earth is the humility beloved of God, before which all ranks of the demons tremble, that virtue into which the demons have not been able to enter.

23.11.6.en: St. Gregory of Cyprus * God will give you knowledge so that you may know Him.

23.11.7.en: St. Stephen of Thebes * The foundation of the monk’s life is true knowledge, and the monk’s ignorance darkens himself.

23.11.8.en: Of St. Hyperechius the Priest * One pilgrim met another pilgrim in the wilderness of Sinai and asked him: “By what is salvation attained?” He said: “By knowledge of the truth of things, and working according to the truth.” He said to him: “Is he who does not know not saved?” He said: “He is not saved.” He said: “And what is knowledge?” He answered: “That the servant know the truth about his Creator, and from what He created him, and what his end will be. For if he knows that, he will not disobey Him, but will work to please Him throughout his life.” He said: “You have spoken truly,” and then departed.

23.11.9.en: Paradise of the Fathers * If a man knows that he is transgressing the commandment, he shows one proof of knowledge, and he who knows corrects himself.

23.12.0.en: St. Barsanuphius Withhold not correction from the child: for if thou beatest him with the rod, he shall not die [13].

23.13.0.en: Thou shalt beat him with the rod, and shalt deliver his soul from hell [14].

23.13.1.en: Discipline with wisdom and love benefits children, for though they suffer a little for a time, it keeps them from falling into the pit.

23.13.2.en: God in His fatherhood to us disciplines us, not out of vengeance but out of kindness toward us and compassion on us for our edification, for the wise man says: “For whom the Lord loveth he correcteth; even as a father the son in whom he delighteth” (Prov 12:3). Firmness in fatherhood differs from the cruelty that lacks fatherhood, for it springs from sincere love.

23.13.3.en: We must bear in mind that before we discipline, our heart must be enlarged with love, as St. Augustine says: [Rebuke must be preceded by mercy, not by anger.]

23.13.4.en: * Correction by discipline, as their names (that is, correction and discipline) imply, is blows that have their effect upon the soul, so that they restrain sin, guard against death, and lead those enslaved by vice to self-control.

23.13.5.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * Just as little children who are neglectful in learning become more alert and obedient after being punished by their teacher or trainer, and just as they do not listen before they are beaten, but after feeling the pain of the beating they hear and respond as though their ears had been newly opened, and progress takes place in their memory, so also with those who neglect the divine teaching and lightly resist the commandments. For after they experience God’s correction of them by discipline, the commandments of God, which were always known to them yet which they neglected, are received with great readiness, as with newly washed ears.

23.13.6.en: St. Basil the Great * Fathers, teach your children in the Lord, and bring them up with discipline and the knowledge of Christ, and teach them fitting trades, lest they be accused of idleness...

23.13.7.en: Do not be afraid to rebuke them and teach them with authority, for you do not kill them if you teach them, but you love them.

23.14.s.en: 6. The righteous son makes his father’s heart rejoice

23.14.0.en: My son, if thine heart be wise, my heart shall rejoice, even mine [15].

23.15.0.en: Yea, my reins shall rejoice, when thy lips speak right things [16].

23.15.1.en: After speaking of the necessity of disciplining children, lest the children think that in this there is a kind of disdain of the fathers for them, or contempt for their thinking, or stifling of their breath, he gives us his personal experience with regard to his own sons. He rejoices in their wisdom, and his heart exults in their success through the uprightness of their lives.

23.15.2.en: These are Solomon’s feelings toward his children; how much more are the feelings of God and His joy in the wisdom of His children. He gives His children wisdom, and then boasts in their wisdom and the uprightness of their hearts.

23.15.3.en: Here he urges children not to be angry when they fall under the divine discipline or the discipline of their parents.

23.15.4.en: And why do we speak of the joy of God and of parents in children upright in heart, when even the angels rejoice in them, as appears from the vision of St. Abba Anthony at the departure of St. Abba Paul.

23.15.5.en: * The crucified monk who dies every day acquires great grace, for the angels rejoice in him when he is received into the Kingdom of Heaven.

23.15.6.en: * How great is the joy of the angels when they see a sinner enter the Kingdom of Heaven by his repentance! And how great is the delight of the saints when they find a sinner turning back from his error! So after you imitate their faith, seek diligently the joy that follows it.

23.15.7.en: St. Hyperechius the Priest * (On the meeting of Abba Anthony with Abba Paul) Abba Anthony returned by the same road by which he had come, longing to see Abba Paul before he gave up his spirit to Christ, but on his way he saw a company of angels and in their midst St. Paul as they were taking him up, and they were praising and saying:

23.15.8.en: “Peace upon your meeting with the saints, O Paul, man of God.

23.15.9.en: The angels rejoice with you. You will be glad in the heavens.

23.15.10.en: You have left the darkness behind, and gone forth to the Paradise of bliss.

23.15.11.en: You have left sorrow behind for the joy that has no end.

23.15.12.en: You have left weeping behind, and you will go on to eternal joy.

23.15.13.en: For you have become blessed in your generation, and your memory is through the passing of the ages.

23.15.14.en: You are a man of God; blessed are you, and again blessed.”

23.15.15.en: Paradise of the Fathers * They said to him (to Abba Anthony): “What is the meaning of the Apostle’s saying: ‘Rejoice in the Lord’?” He said: “If we rejoice in doing the commandments, this is rejoicing in the Lord. Let us rejoice in fulfilling the commandments of the Lord and in the success of our brethren, and let us guard ourselves from the joy of the world and from laughter if we want to be of the Lord’s own. For He said that the world will rejoice, and you will weep (Jn 16:20), and He said that woe is to those who laugh and blessed are those who weep (Lk 6:21, 25). And it is not written that He ever laughed, and it is written that He grieved and His eyes shed tears (Jn 11:35).

23.16.s.en: 7. Holding fast to the fear of the Lord

23.16.0.en: 17 Let not thine heart envy sinners: but be thou in the fear of the Lord all the day long. 18 For surely there is an end; and thine expectation shall not be cut off.

23.16.1.en: Let not thine heart envy sinners: but be thou in the fear of the Lord all the day long [17].

23.16.2.en: Some envy the wicked who prosper, but whoever enjoys the fear of the Lord realizes that the success of the wicked is temporary and does not last, and that if they do not return to the Lord they perish. But whoever places his hope in the Lord in a spirit of godliness and the fear of the Lord will surely be rewarded in due time.

23.16.3.en: * Three things make the heart rejoice: distinguishing good from evil, thinking about a matter before it is carried out, and keeping away from cunning. And three things enlighten the mind: doing good to him who has wronged you, patiently enduring what befalls you from your enemies, and ceasing to look with envy at him who is ahead of you in the world.

23.16.4.en: St. Abba Arsenius * Just as fire dries up the moisture of wood and burns it, so the fear of the Lord, when it dwells in a man, dries up his flesh and withers his bones.

23.16.5.en: * There is nothing that rises above the fear of the Lord, for it rules over everything, and by the fear of the Lord everyone departs from all evils. Let us therefore acquire this fear for ourselves, let us turn away from everything that God does not want, and test and keep everything that pleases Him, and do nothing that grieves Him, and know that everything we do He beholds, and nothing is hidden from Him.

23.16.6.en: St. Macarius the Great * In our time we do not find anyone who asks: Who is it that fears the Lord? But rather: Who is the senior by the laying on of hands? And if they say: So-and-so is senior, they say to him: It is fitting for you to sit at the head of the table. And no one remembers the words of the Savior when He pronounced woe on the scribes and Pharisees.

23.17.0.en: St. Aphrahat For surely there is an end; and thine expectation shall not be cut off [18].

23.17.1.en: At the same time that the wise man warns us not to envy the wicked for the progress, success or abundance of goods they have attained, because these are temporary things, he asks us to fix our eyes on the hope of obtaining the eternal inheritance, true success and lasting victory. For the true believer, hope opens the doors of heaven before his eyes, so he lives rejoicing under all the circumstances of life, however harsh they may seem. He is confident in the riches of God’s grace and the possibility of enjoying a life of victory.

23.17.2.en: * Do not be fainthearted, O monk who labors in the virtues, and say in your heart: My enemies have caught me for nothing like a bird. Know that the victory of Jesus is with you at all times, and cry out with joy, and say: The Lord is my help; whom shall I fear? Knock at the door of His tenderness, and He will answer you quickly. Ask Him your petition in faith, and He will give you His mercies many times over, and do not say: I cannot work.

23.17.3.en: * What dries up all the crops of Satan is prayer with hope in God.

23.17.4.en: * If the demon of dejection comes upon them (the believers), let them be comforted by the promises of our Lord, and look to the hope of the riches of the Spirit, and surrender themselves to the promises of joy. By this the sorrows of dejection will pass from them with God’s help, and His joy will dwell in their souls.

23.17.5.en: * Flee from the counsels of the demon of dejection and from the cutting off of hope, and listen with love to these discernments that we have set down for you: Christ is merciful, so seek Him with all your hearts, and be strengthened, and He will heal the pains of your bodies and the sicknesses of your souls. Do not fear, O laborer, and do not tremble at the threats of the demons. For they are scattered before the power of virtue. You who have been overcome by the demons, work and live, and do not cut off your hope.

23.17.6.en: If you have sinned like the thief, cry out to our Lord: “Remember me,” and you will live; or if you have fallen like the harlot, go out in search of the mercy of our Lord and you will find it. Do not fear, and do not rest from seeking mercy. Flee from thoughts of cutting off hope.

23.18.0.en: 19 Hear thou, my son, and be wise, and guide thine heart in the way. 20 Be not among winebibbers; among those who destroy their own bodies: 21 For the drunkard and the prodigal shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags.

23.18.1.en: Hear thou, my son, and be wise, and guide thine heart in the way [19].

23.18.2.en: In the spirit of tender fatherhood the wise man declares that he does not seek to deprive his son of anything, but that when he forbids him to be addicted to wine or to excess in bodily pleasures, it is only in order that his son may walk with wisdom in the straight way, for the good of his body, soul and spirit.

23.18.3.en: He warns him against the company of drunkards and those immersed in excess and pleasures, for the company of the wicked impels one to share in their evils.

23.19.0.en: Be not among winebibbers; among those who destroy their own bodies [20].

23.20.0.en: For the drunkard and the prodigal shall come to poverty: and drowsiness shall clothe a man with rags [21].

23.20.1.en: St. Gregory, bishop of Nyssa, sees that it is fitting for the believer to obey the commandment of the Lord Christ to put off the old garment (Mk 21:2), the tattered garment worn by him who is drunk with wine and by the harlot (Prov 21:23), in order to put on the new garment, the garment of purity and immortality, after the likeness of the garment of the Lord Christ in which He appeared at His Transfiguration. * The Fathers said: “Where there is wine drinking... there is no need for a demon.”

23.20.2.en: * An elder said: “It is good for your name to be found written in the houses of the poor and widows and the weak, rather than found written in the houses of wine sellers. And it is good for your mouth to smell foul from the severity of fasting, rather than for its smell to be that of wine.”

23.20.3.en: * The monks were celebrating one of the feasts in Scetis, and they gave one of the elders a cup of wine, and he refused it, saying: “Take this death away from me.” When the others who were eating with him saw what he had done, they too refused to take any wine.

23.20.4.en: Paradise of the Fathers * Above all the monk must avoid gatherings with women and the drinking of wine, for wine and women make even the wise fall (Sir 19:2).

23.21.0.en: Hearken unto thy father that begat thee, and despise not thy mother when she is old [22].

23.21.1.en: It was said of the Lord Christ: “Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered” (Heb 8:5). And we, as members of His body, when we are united with Him, are rightly counted obedient, since we bear fellowship in His features. On the other hand, we understand obedience not as servility and humiliation or a diminishing of our worth, but as union with Christ, who obeyed the Father while being one with Him in essence, and obeyed St. Mary and St. Joseph, who were the work of His hands. Thus we understand true obedience as union with the Lord Christ and maturity.

23.21.2.en: * The Scripture says, “He was subject unto them.” To whom was Jesus subject? Was He not subject to His parents? As the Son of Man He was subject to both of His parents (St. Joseph, His father according to the Law, and St. Mary, His mother)...

23.21.3.en: Let children learn their commandments: which are obedience and submission to their parents. For the world was subject to Christ, and Christ was subject to His parents.

23.22.0.en: Buy the truth, and sell it not; also wisdom, and instruction, and understanding [23].

23.22.1.en: * May we hunger for righteousness and be filled (Mt 5:6) from the table of His Kingdom. Let us be the salt of the truth, so that we do not become food for the serpent. Let us clear our seed of thorns, so that we may bring forth fruit a hundredfold (Lk 8:7-8).

23.22.2.en: Let us set our building upon the rock (Mt 7:24), so that it is not shaken by winds and waves.

23.22.3.en: Let us be vessels unto honour (2 Tim 2:21), so that the Lord may seek us for His use.

23.22.4.en: Let us sell all that we have and buy for ourselves the pearl (Mt 13:46), and so be enriched.

23.22.5.en: * Let us gird our loins with truth, so that we are not found weak in the battle.

23.23.s.en: 11. The parents’ joy in the righteous son

23.23.0.en: The father of the righteous shall greatly rejoice: and he that begetteth a wise child shall have joy of him [24].

23.24.0.en: Thy father and thy mother shall be glad, and she that bare thee shall rejoice [25].

23.24.1.en: When the life of Saul of Tarsus changed and he enjoyed the new holy life, he says: “And they glorified God in me” (Gal 1:24). This is the attitude of the Church, which exulted in the life of Saul (the Apostle Paul), who became her son. In the same spirit the hearts of parents are filled with inexpressible joy when they see in their children the righteousness of Christ and the wisdom of God working in their lives, and their souls are refreshed, as they see that God has listened to their prayers for their children, sanctified their lives, and removed from them sinful habits that they used to practice.

23.25.0.en: My son, give me thine heart, and let thine eyes observe my ways [26].

23.25.1.en: The most that God wants from us is the heart. In the Old Testament the Law was given to us engraved on stones, that our stony hearts might catch something of the divine Law, or that the Law might leave its imprints on our hearts. And since this did not happen, the Gospel of the New Testament gave us a law carved by the Holy Spirit on our hearts. “I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts” (Heb 10:8). Therefore when the priest cries out: “Lift up your hearts,” the people sing exultantly: “We lift them up unto the Lord.”

23.25.2.en: * Within you is either the knowledge of the truth or ignorance, delight in virtue or in vice; by this we prepare our hearts either for the Kingdom of Christ or the kingdom of the devil.

23.25.3.en: Father Moses * If you do not give your soul, you lose it. Love itself speaks through wisdom, and tells you, in order to save you from a state of panic, as it is said: “Give me your soul.” If someone wants to sell you a field, he says to you: “Give me your gold,” and if it is something else he says to you: “Give me your copper,” “Give me your silver.” Now listen to what love says to you, speaking through the mouth of wisdom: “My son, give me thine heart.” What do you give it? “Your heart, my son.” Your heart was evil when it was with you, when you kept it for yourself. You were drawn this way and that as by dolls and trifles and the lusts of destructive love. Cast your heart away from all this. Where are you drawing it? Where are you putting it? Wisdom says: “Give me thine heart.” Make it mine, and you will not lose it.

23.26.0.en: For a whore is a deep ditch; and a strange woman is a narrow pit [27].

23.27.0.en: She also lieth in wait as for a prey, and increaseth the transgressors among men [28].

23.27.1.en: There is no virtue greater than purity and cleanness, so that a person sees in the other sex brothers or sisters, whom he respects as persons, and not as objects for the satisfaction of his evil lusts. Therefore it is fitting for a person to flee from stumbling, lest he fall into adultery, even in thought or even in dreams, or later in moments of his weakness. The enemy of good wishes, if possible, to corrupt the purity of every person, even if he is a hermit ascetic.

23.27.2.en: * Solomon compares the love of such a woman to a deep pit. She calls the one who loves her lame when she sees that he has lost all his possessions (that is, she mocks him and the poverty that has befallen him because of her). And she does not stop at this, but opposes him with all her effort without ceasing and causes his collapse, and mocks him, and causes him many troubles, things which words cannot describe.

23.27.3.en: St. John Chrysostom * Woe to the unjust, for his wealth flees from him and an unquenchable fire meets him. Woe to the negligent, for they wish for the time they neglected and do not find it. Woe to the lover of fornication, for he goes out from the king’s wedding feast in shame. Woe to the deceiver and the drunkard, for they are condemned with murderers and adulterers. Woe to him who respects persons, for the shepherd will deny him and the wolves will devour him.

23.27.4.en: St. Nilus of Sinai * If we keep the right faith and keep the body from fornication and the tongue from slander, then by the grace of God we are prospering according to this age.

23.27.5.en: Abba Palla * A brother asked an elder about thoughts of fornication, saying: “What shall I do about the thought of fornication that troubles me?” Father Copres of Alexandria answered, saying: “Cast yourself down in prayer before God, for if we had no thoughts we would be mere animals. Just as the enemy works for what is his, so let us work for what is ours. Let us stand in prayer and let us care for our faith, and let us endure, for enduring with patience is itself a victory. And if a man does not strive he will never be crowned. For there are champions in the world who win in spite of their wounds, and although two persons may wound one person many times, if he can endure the blows he can triumph over the two who struck him. Observe what degree of endurance those who work for trade in this world possess! So you too endure, and God will fight against your enemies on your behalf while you remain quiet.”

23.27.6.en: Paradise of the Fathers * The demon of fornication stirs up bodily lust, and launches his attack on the ascetics, and strives to make them abandon their asceticism, sowing in their souls that this asceticism of theirs is of no use.

23.27.7.en: And if he is able to defile the soul, he begins to prepare it to speak some (evil) talk and to listen to it, so that it seems as though the (evil) deed itself is present before their eyes.

23.27.8.en: * The demon of vainglory is opposed to the demon of fornication. And it is not possible for the two to fight the soul together. For one promises honour and dignity, and the other brings shame. Therefore if one of them draws near to you and begins to trouble you, call to mind the thoughts you were exposed to from the opposing demon; and if you succeed in what the proverb says about driving out a nail with a nail, know that you are on the way to being without passion (free from lust), if you prove that your mind is able to drive away the counsels of the demon concerning human thoughts.

23.27.9.en: But of course, if you are able to drive away the thought of vainglory by humility, and the thought of fornication by chastity, this is a sign that you are “free from passion.”

23.27.10.en: Try also to do this with all the demons and their opposites, and ask God to help and assist you, so that you may drive away the enemies by the second method (resorting to humility and chastity, etc.).

23.28.0.en: 29 Who hath woe? who hath sorrow? who hath contentions? who hath distress? who hath wounds without cause? who hath redness of eyes? 30 They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine. 31 Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it goeth down smoothly. 32 At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder. 33 Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things. 34 Yea, thou shalt be as he that lieth down in the midst of the sea, or as he that lieth upon the top of a mast. 35 They have stricken me, shalt thou say, and I was not sick; they have beaten me, and I knew it not: when shall I awake? I will seek it yet again.

23.28.4.en: who hath distress? who hath wounds without cause?

23.28.6.en: The wise man presents us with six brief questions, and the answer to them comes in the following verses, which give a terrifying description of the life of the drunkard.

23.29.0.en: They that tarry long at the wine; they that go to seek mixed wine [30].

23.30.0.en: Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it goeth down smoothly [31].

23.30.1.en: * With reference to the redness of the eyes, a sign of death, it is clear that the bubbling of wine is indeed death to the Word and to reason. It proclaims his death to the Lord. When a man forgets the motives that urge him to seek the true life, he is drawn down toward corruption. Therefore, for a good reason, the Teacher who cares for our salvation strictly forbids us: “Be not drunk with wine.”

23.30.2.en: St. Clement of Alexandria * Understand this, brethren: every drunkard makes the habit of drinking an inner leprosy in the soul, for the soul of the drunkard is known to be like the body of the leper. Therefore whoever wishes to be free from the sin of drunkenness, which kills the soul and weakens the body, must drink little. Whoever does not keep this rule is hated by God and an object of men’s mockery.

23.30.3.en: * Those who want to be like this (drunkards) try in a wretched way to find an excuse for themselves. They say: My friend will be upset if I do not give him what he wants to drink when I invite him to a banquet. [But I say to you,] let there be no friend of yours who wants to make you displeasing to God, for he is an enemy to himself as well as to you. If you make yourself like other drunkards, you will have a man as a friend, and God as an enemy to you.

23.31.0.en: Father Caesarius, bishop of Arles At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder [32].

23.31.1.en: Drunkenness is one of the great plagues that afflict humanity, and causes it misery. Though all recognize its danger, it nevertheless attracts many and leads them astray. The wise man likens it to a poisonous serpent that a man embraces and it destroys him.

23.31.2.en: * It was said of Abba Paphnutius that he did not drink wine even when he was ill.

23.31.3.en: * Brethren asked an elder: “What is the meaning of Abba Sisoes’ saying that the third cup is from Satan?” The elder said: “That is because he knew that excess is the cause of all sins: abuse, striking, fornication and the rest of the passions. Therefore we must avoid drinking wine not only because of the passions, but also because of the relaxation it brings into our hearts, so that the demons find the opportunity to draw us into sin and deprive us of the blessedness that our Lord promised to those who mourn. The hermits withdrew in order to mourn at all times and to labor in every work, for with much sorrow they are able to keep their souls from the deceit of the demons and the multitude of battles; so how could they drink much wine that gladdens their hearts and looses their seals, and fall into the sins of drunken laymen?!”

23.32.0.en: Paradise of the Fathers Thine eyes shall behold strange women, and thine heart shall utter perverse things [33].

23.32.1.en: Drunkenness inflames in a man bodily lusts that cause him to lose his purity and the uprightness of his life. It also stirs in his depths a state of disturbance and imbalance, which is often reflected even in his conduct, so that he loses his balance.

23.32.2.en: * Whoever allows himself to drink wine cannot escape the assault of thoughts and the ugliness of deeds, for when Lot was compelled by his two daughters and became drunk with wine, it was easy for Satan to cause him to fall into the ugly act of fornication.

23.32.3.en: Abba Isidore * An elder said: “Wine stirs up the desire for procreation and gladdens the heart (humanly), and dispels sorrow (in a soulish, bodily way), as the wise Solomon said: ‘Give strong drink unto him that is ready to perish, and wine unto those that be of heavy hearts. Let him drink, and forget his poverty, and remember his misery no more’ (Prov 31:6-7).’”
